newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary shrs merit better weight in C.Europe - HSBC.
newsitem.headline: Hungary shrs merit better weight in C.Europe - HSBC.

text.p: Investors should boost Hungary's proportion within their central European portfolios and focus more on domestically-oriented firms, HSBC James Capel suggested in a country report dated March 26.
"We believe that investors should overweight the Hungarian equity market relative to the rest of Central Europe," wrote Nigel Rendell, emerging markets strategist at HSBC James Capel in London.
"The main positives are a pick-up in domestic demand, attractive valuation and, over the medium term, declining interest rates," he added.
Rendell said the Hungarian share market offered further growth potential.
"From a little over 5,000 at present, we expect the BUX index to rise towards 7,500 points by the year-end, giving a potential upside of around 33 percent in dollar terms," he said.
"With the corporate sector benefiting from a pick-up in the domestic economy, we see the equity market returning to vogue."
On Wednesday the BUX index closed at 5,281.76 points, while it reached its all-time high of 5,815.38 points on February 5.
As well as the large cap stocks, investors would concentrate on the domestically-oriented companies, HSBC suggested.

Tile maker Zalakeramia remained on HSBC's buy list after its recent acquisitions, plastics maker Pannonplast was also well placed, while home improvement product maker Graboplast was a quality company, he said.
He added that Graboplast, a "hold" when its price was 8,250 forints, presented a good longer-term buying opportunity at 7,700 forints.
The market's large cap stocks, oil and gas company MOL, pharmaceutical Richter and chemicals Borsodchem and OTP Bank, were expected to continue to do well, HSBC's Rendell said.

Hungary's economic outlook for 1997 was somewhat brighter with the period of real wage declines having come to and end, and encouraged by lower interest rates, private consumption should register positive growth for the first time in three years, he said.

"Prospects for a further decline in inflation during the coming year are good, although the rate of decline will be substantially less than last year," Rendell said, adding that over the coming months the inflation profile would be hit by higher energy prices.
